emhawkes

emhawkes specifies, simulates, and fits exponential Hawkes models, including marked, state-dependent, and multi-kernel models.

library(emhawkes)

h <- new("hspec",
  mu = c(0.2, 0.2),
  alpha = matrix(c(0.5, 0.9, 0.9, 0.5), 2, byrow = TRUE),
  beta = matrix(2.25, 2, 2)
)
set.seed(1107)
path <- hsim(h, size = 1000)
fit <- hfit(h, path$inter_arrival, path$type)
summary(fit)

Use fitted_hspec(fit) to restore the estimated model and fit_initial_state(fit) to retrieve the initial-state arguments:

estimated <- fitted_hspec(fit)
initial <- fit_initial_state(fit)
inferred <- do.call(logLik, c(list(object = estimated,
  inter_arrival = path$inter_arrival, type = path$type, mark = path$mark,
  infer = TRUE), initial))

The result remains a maxLik object, so coef(), summary(), and vcov() keep their existing behavior. The saved parameter map preserves shared parameters and fixed constants in component functions. Simulation generators are retained, and their named parameters are updated when they match estimated coefficient names. Automatic initial intensity remains NULL and is recalculated for the restored model. Initial counts are retained. A custom objective is not incorporated into the restored model.

Save the fit with saveRDS() to retain this information between sessions. Keep the observed data separately and supply them again for inference. The stored optimization objective can retain data in its function environment. The saved initial state describes the start of the observation window. Pass it to hsim() to start a new path from the estimated model. Continuing after the last observed event requires that event’s state. Fits created without the new metadata need to be refitted before using the reconstruction helpers.

By default, hfit() uses the final Hessian and standard errors from maxLik. It does not run the additional stabilization checks. If numerical Hawkes standard errors contain NaN, a short message suggests trying final_hessian = "stable". Request this option to check numerical Hawkes curvature with scaled central differences and Richardson extrapolation. This preserves the optimizer’s coefficients and log-likelihood. summary() and vcov() then use the checked covariance; free-parameter standard errors are NA when stable inversion is unavailable. Inspect fit_diagnostics(fit) for the requested checks. Supplied Hessians, disabled final curvature, BHHH, custom objectives, and residual models retain their calculation choices.

The fit also records its calculation methods:

calculation <- fit_diagnostics(fit)$computation
calculation$engine   # Requested engine, actual engines and auto fallback reason.
calculation$gradient # Numeric, analytic or user-supplied score.
calculation$hessian # Requested and applied final-Hessian methods.

An auto fit can record both "cpp" and "r" if it switches during estimation. The record includes final curvature evaluations and survives saveRDS(). Older fits without this record return recorded = FALSE and NA for unrecorded methods. The existing curvature checks remain available at the top level.

A stable Hessian does not guarantee reliable Wald intervals. Nearby kernel decay rates, weak excitation, boundaries, short samples, and nonsmooth callbacks can still make inference unreliable. The Hawkes standard-error report compares unchanged estimates and corrected standard errors, and discusses profile likelihood and bootstrap. The earlier diagnostic report records the original Hawkes and FRPP issues.

By default, reduced = TRUE treats equal starting values within each parameter matrix as one parameter. This example estimates four parameters: one for mu, two for alpha, and one for beta. hfit() explains this rule once before optimization.

Use reduced = FALSE to estimate the ten matrix entries separately, even when their starting values are equal. Function components share parameters by name under either setting. A zero in a numeric matrix is also a starting value; use a component function to fix selected entries at zero.

The first data row is the initial state. inter_arrival, type, and mark start with zero, followed by the observed events. hsim(size) includes this initial row. N0 and Nc0 specify initial counts and mark totals; Nc0 must be named in hfit().

The likelihood ends at the last supplied event. N0 and Nc0 accept a scalar or one value per event type. Supplied N and Nc matrices must agree with the event data and initial counts. Explicit type_col_map requires initial kernel components for simulation and the built-in likelihood.

logLik(h, ..., infer = TRUE) returns a list with the likelihood, intensity paths, and residual vectors. Use it in place of the deprecated infer_lambda() and residual_process() helpers. Simulation returns an hreal object.

With automatic engine selection, numeric Hawkes specifications use a compiled Rcpp engine for likelihood evaluation and inference, including multi-kernel models, unequal decay rates, and numeric mark effects. Standalone likelihood and inference also support parameter-only component functions returning plain numeric matrices. Observed baselines and observed or sequential state-dependent impacts also use C++. Baselines cannot depend on latent intensities. Unsupported function signatures use R. Mark densities, residual-distribution models, and numeric inputs with custom classes use R. Simulation continues to use R. The fitting adapters below also select C++ automatically for supported callback models.

hfit() uses this engine for its built-in likelihood. Numerical differentiation remains the default. For numeric Hawkes models, request the Rcpp analytic gradient:

fit <- hfit(h, path$inter_arrival, path$type, gradient = "analytic")

This option supports shared and fixed parameters, multi-kernel mappings, numeric mark effects, and derivatives of automatic initial states. It computes the likelihood and score together. State-dependent baselines and impacts that use latent intensities, custom likelihoods, mark densities, residual distributions, equality constraints, and BHHH are not yet supported. Singular automatic initialization requires explicit lambda_component0. A supplied grad takes precedence. A supplied hess is retained; otherwise maxLik can differentiate the analytic gradient for curvature. The optimizer’s path and last digits may differ from numerical differentiation. The gradient report describes accuracy, full-fit timings, and the state-dependent extension.

Parameter-only mu, alpha, beta, and eta functions can also use the analytic option when supplied with their exact Jacobians. For example, this function fixes one excitation entry at zero:

alpha_fun <- function(param = c(a = 0.2, b = 0.1)) {
  matrix(c(param["a"], 0, param["b"], param["a"]), 2)
}
alpha_jac <- cbind(a = c(1, 0, 0, 1), b = c(0, 0, 1, 0))
h_fun <- new("hspec", mu = h@mu, alpha = alpha_fun, beta = h@beta)
fit_fun <- hfit(h_fun, path$inter_arrival, path$type,
  gradient = "analytic", jacobian = list(alpha = alpha_jac))

Jacobian rows follow as.vector() of the returned matrix; columns are named with its param names. For nonlinear transformations, supply a function(param) that returns the Jacobian at that parameter vector. Components and Jacobians must be deterministic functions of param with fixed matrix dimensions. The package does not derive or verify the formulas automatically. A component with param = numeric(0) needs no Jacobian. Shared parameter names receive the sum of all component contributions. Missing or malformed Jacobians produce an error. The analytic fit evaluates component functions in R and the likelihood and scores in Rcpp. With the default "auto" engine, supported function-valued models also use C++ with numerical differentiation, without Jacobians:

fit_numeric <- hfit(h_fun, path$inter_arrival, path$type)

The functions must return plain numeric matrices of constant dimensions and be deterministic in param. Observed-state impact functions also use this numerical path without Jacobians, including count- and mark-dependent impacts and the Hawkes flocking example. Numerical C++ fitting also supports observed baselines and sequential impacts that explicitly request current or historical intensity states, including the bid-ask example. Mark densities and residual distributions remain unsupported. Supplied grad and hess are retained. Automatic selection uses R for unsupported specifications; forcing "cpp" reports unsupported features. Callback errors propagate. Callbacks must be deterministic with fixed captures; detecting an unsupported state read through ... can require a retry in R. Standalone logLik() and infer = TRUE also use C++ for parameter-only component functions, observed baselines, and observed or sequential state-dependent impacts. The default automatic selection therefore accelerates replay of restored models with these components. Each callback keeps its own defaults; standalone replay does not apply parameter-sharing rules from fitting.

Observed-state impact functions can use the analytic option with jacobian = list(impact = impact_jac). They may depend on observed N, Nc, marks, types, and times, and on the resolved mu, alpha, and beta matrices. Counts at row n include that event. The event’s impact affects subsequent intensities in the kernel columns selected by its type.

For jacobian$impact, param is the full named optimization vector. Return a matrix with one row per impact entry in column-major order and one named column per fitted parameter, including zero columns. Include derivatives through any core matrices used by the impact. The impact function keeps receiving its local parameters. See ?hfit for an example and the callback contract. Callbacks that read latent intensities remain unsupported by the analytic option. Default numerical fitting uses C++ for supported callbacks. Declare lambda_component_n to receive the current pre-jump component matrix. Declare lambda or lambda_component only when full pre-jump histories are needed. Observed baselines may use counts and marks, return a dimensions-by-one matrix, and remain constant between events. They cannot depend on latent intensities. See the bid-ask benchmark for the state convention, compatibility checks and timings.

When only the current state is needed, use lambda_component_n. Full histories need storage proportional to events times dimensions times kernels. If a callback retains these histories, snapshot-preserving copies can make cumulative copying grow quadratically with event count. Peak live memory and cumulative allocation are different costs. See the scaling measurements for time, allocation and memory comparisons.

See the count, mark and flocking benchmark for complete-fit timings and accuracy checks.

The emhawkes.engine option controls the built-in likelihood:

Setting Role
"auto" (default) Use C++ for supported models and R otherwise. Supported fitting adapters receive this acceleration automatically.
"r" Force the R likelihood for comparison or troubleshooting.
"cpp" Require C++ support; report an error for unsupported models.

Setting "cpp" is unnecessary to accelerate models already supported by "auto". Inspect fit_diagnostics(fit)$computation$engine for the engines actually used and any automatic fallback reason. Engine selection does not enable analytic gradients: request gradient = "analytic" explicitly; unsupported analytic gradients produce an error. A custom mylogLik bypasses built-in engine selection. Installing from source requires a C++ compiler and Rcpp; Windows source installations require Rtools.
